title: Welcome to VECTOR
focus: One call. One incident. A complete workflow.
narration: Every response begins with information. A call. A location. A decision. This is Vector: the dispatch and mobile data terminal interface for your emergency-service simulator. Bring calls, incident assessment, searches and resource control into one workspace. Follow a fictional incident from the first alert to mobilisation, then into the crew terminal. This is the current demonstration build. Welcome to Vector.

title: Orientate your workspace
focus: The map is your main workspace
narration: Start on Dispatch. The map provides the central workspace, with calls, live incidents and resources available in surrounding panels. The main navigation takes you to the nine nine nine call page, the mobilisation screen and Ground. Before starting, identify the selected incident reference. That reference provides context for the information and resource controls you are about to use.

title: One workspace. Multiple screens.
focus: Detach the map and any floating panel
steps: Pop out • move between displays • dock back
narration: Your workspace is not limited to one screen. Use the pop out control to open a floating panel or the map in its own window. Move that window to another display using its operating system title bar. Keep the call on your main screen and the map alongside. This staged two-display animation illustrates the tested pop out behaviour. Dock back restores the panel.

title: Recognise an incoming call
focus: An incoming call must remain visible
steps: Banner + call stack + persistent alert strip
narration: When a new call arrives, the pop up banner brings it to your attention even when the call panel is closed. Read the service, reported nature, location and waiting information before answering. The persistent alert strip provides another route back to waiting calls. In this demonstration, Test call produces an example arrival. It is not a connection to a telephone network.

title: Answer and establish context
focus: Confirm which call you are handling
steps: Active caller • reported nature • callback details
narration: Answering opens the call handling page and removes that call from the unanswered stack. Check the active call identity, the reported problem and any caller details supplied. Do not assume missing information has been verified elsewhere. The example concerns smoke issuing from a dwelling. Keep the distinction between what the caller has reported and what has actually been confirmed.

title: Read the location evidence
focus: A location fix is evidence to check
narration: Next, look at the location source. The interface can display handset location information and other location references. Read the source and any accuracy information alongside the caller's description. A marker identifies a possible location; it does not prove which building or entrance is involved. If sources disagree, resolve that disagreement before treating the address as a confirmed incident location.

title: Select and confirm an address
focus: Choose the correct record, then confirm it
narration: The compact address control is designed for a quick, deliberate choice. Select the matching address, check the building number, street and locality with the caller, then use Confirm address. Add useful access details in the separate field. The confirmed state should reflect a completed check, rather than simply accepting whichever search result happens to appear first in the list.

title: Search when the match is unclear
focus: Expand search only when you need it
narration: If the suggested address is wrong or ambiguous, expand Search or change address. Compare the available records and their supporting details, then return to the compact confirmation step. Similar street names, nearby properties and a different access point can all matter. For an unclear location, preserve the uncertainty in the record instead of making the display appear more precise than the information allows.

title: Use the triage questions
focus: Ask, record and reassess
narration: The triage area groups questions around the nature of the incident, risks, casualties, access and caller updates. In this prototype, pressing Ask inserts a scripted question and reply into the dialogue. In a connected system, the operator would record the caller's actual response. Work through the relevant questions and distinguish a direct observation from information the caller heard from somebody else.

title: Keep the dialogue useful
focus: Record what changed and what remains unknown
narration: The dialogue provides a chronological account of the call. Use it to follow what has been asked and what new information changes your understanding. In our example, reports about a person inside require careful attribution. Unknown is different from no. Keep checking for meaningful changes, while avoiding repeated questions that add no useful information to the incident record.

title: Do not wait for every question
focus: Incomplete triage does not block mobilisation
narration: The question counter is a progress guide, not a requirement to finish every question before mobilising. This interface allows creation when the essential call, location and incident type checks are satisfied, even with questions remaining. That does not mean skipping those essential checks. It means you can progress the response while continuing relevant information gathering as the call develops.

title: Escalate with a reason
focus: Keep escalation beside the call assessment
narration: Use Escalate call when the assessment needs a higher priority or a review. Record the reason so the change is understandable to the next operator. If the call already has the highest available priority, the interface can represent a request for supervisor review. In this prototype that request is recorded locally; it does not notify a real supervisor or another control room.

title: Open the Systems workspace
focus: Choose the system for the question
steps: Address Check • Premises Risk • Incident History
narration: The Systems menu brings enquiries into a separate movable window. Choose the system that answers your current question rather than opening every tool. Address Check helps inspect an address record. Premises Risk and Incident History provide additional context in this demonstration. Keep the active incident reference in view when copying information between the call screen and an enquiry window.

title: Check risk and previous incidents
focus: Use context without confusing it with this call
steps: Recorded hazards are not newly confirmed facts
narration: Premises information can help identify recorded access issues or hazards, while incident history shows earlier events associated with a location. Those records add context; they do not establish what is happening now. Compare the address carefully and distinguish historical information from the current caller's report. The records shown here are demonstration content, with live data connections still to be added.

title: Use PNC and copy controls
focus: Copy the exact value into the right enquiry
narration: For a relevant policing enquiry, select P N C and choose the appropriate record view. Copy controls are intended to reduce retyping of registrations, names, numbers and identifiers. Check the value and search context before using it. The P N C screen here contains clearly fictional sample records. It demonstrates the layout and copying workflow, not access to the Police National Computer.

title: Read ANPR results in context
focus: A recorded sighting is not a live location
narration: The A N P R page presents a vehicle read history. Compare the registration, time, camera location and direction, then select a row for its details. A historic read is not proof of the vehicle's current position. The example uses fictional training reads and has no camera image. It shows how a result could be inspected without claiming a live tracking connection.

title: Bring in a second service
focus: Add Ambulance alongside Fire
steps: Select incident type • ADD Ambulance • review attendance
narration: Some calls need more than one service. In our fire example, the reported risk to people may also require an ambulance response in the scenario. Select the incident type, then use Add beside Ambulance to include that service alongside Fire. Review the updated attendance preview. Add is different from Pass over: it keeps the current call while including another service in this simulated attendance.

title: Create the incident once
focus: One call creates one incident
steps: Use the existing incident for subsequent updates
narration: After checking the location, incident type and multi-service attendance, select Create incident and mobilise. Vector creates one incident reference and opens the allocation screen. Returning to the same call shows Incident created, with a separate option to view mobilisation. Continue updating that existing incident. Adding a second service is not a reason to create another copy of the same incident from this call.

title: Allocate suitable resources
focus: Allocation is not the same as sending
narration: On Mobilising, review each required attendance slot. Allocate a suitable available resource, checking its type and existing commitments. In this example, a resource is placed into a matching slot while other requirements remain unfilled. A selected callsign means it has been allocated. It has not necessarily received instructions, accepted the task or started moving towards the incident.

title: Send and monitor acknowledgements
focus: Follow the whole mobilisation sequence
steps: Sent → received → accepted → turning out → mobile
narration: Send the mobilisation message, then monitor the acknowledgement sequence. Sent, received, accepted, turning out and mobile are separate stages. This prototype provides controls to simulate those crew replies. A lack of acceptance is visibly flagged after the demonstration timeout. Do not interpret that example timeout as a universal service standard; the connected system should apply its own configured operational rules.

title: Keep shortfalls visible
focus: An unfilled slot remains an outstanding need
narration: An incomplete attendance remains visible after the allocated resources are sent. Continue to track unfilled requirements and review the effect of commitments on available cover. Available units, attendance and county cover panels support different parts of that picture. Sending some resources should not make the remaining requirements disappear. The incident needs to remain understandable to the next operator taking over the desk.

title: Control a selected resource
focus: Select the unit, then use its MDT
narration: Back on Dispatch, select an incident and then choose a resource from its map marker or Scene Units row. The rugged M D T window opens with the callsign and incident reference clearly displayed. Actions are tailored to the resource. The window can be moved, resized or minimised, keeping the map usable while you work with that unit's controls.

title: Assign crew and follow the task
focus: Check availability before starting
narration: Choose an action and select the crew required for it. The preview checks its local crew availability and shows active tasks with a way to release those crew. The main simulation contains richer capability and equipment rules which still need connecting to this interface. The Incident and Messages tabs keep context close by; message sending here creates a local demonstration record only.

title: Complete the handover
focus: Leave a clear incident record
narration: To finish, review the incident reference, confirmed location, recorded risks, resource status and anything still outstanding. End the call when appropriate in the workflow; ending a call does not mean the incident is resolved. The sequence is receive, confirm location, triage, make relevant enquiries, create once, allocate, send and monitor. That is the core Vector journey demonstrated in this introduction.
